title: HelioHealth x Redwood — POC scoping (Dedicated inference + rollout/change mgmt)
summary: POC scoping call focused on HelioHealth’s requirements for predictable rollouts (no silent model changes), version pinning, and customer-visible release notes for any model/version update. Redwood walked through Hosted vs Dedicated deployment options, current and planned model changelog approach (metadata schema + automated release notes + feeds), and operational controls (canaries, fallback, audit trail). HelioHealth emphasized regulated workflow needs (change approval, evidence for audits) and asked for a machine-readable changelog plus SLA/notice windows. Agreed on a 2–3 week Dedicated POC with pinned versions, defined eval prompts, and a weekly rollout review cadence; Redwood to share docs/screenshots of the upcoming changelog UX and sample release-note format.
topics: Customer-visible model release notes / changelog feed
POC plan: dataset, eval prompts, latency/throughput targets
questions: Can Redwood guarantee no behavior changes when a model version is pinned?
How will we be notified when Redwood updates a model version or deprecates one?
Do release notes include compatibility notes (tools/function calling, context window changes)?
Can we export release notes for our internal change-control board (CAB) process?
Can Dedicated be configured for canary rollouts and automated fallback?
next_steps: Redwood (Paula) to send proposed POC plan (timeline, success metrics, rollout cadence) by 2026-02-16
Redwood (Elliot) to share sample customer-facing model release note template + style guidance by 2026-02-18
Redwood (Quentin) to confirm candidate models for HelioHealth workload (chat + summarization) and recommend baseline + fallback variants by 2026-02-17
HelioHealth (Miguel) to provide 30–50 representative prompts + expected outputs/heuristics for eval by 2026-02-20
HelioHealth (Priya) to send their change-management notification requirements (notice window, required fields) by 2026-02-19
Schedule a 60-min technical deep dive on Dedicated rollouts + audit logs the week of 2026-02-17
transcript:
Fireflies.ai — Transcript

Meeting title: HelioHealth x Redwood — POC scoping (Dedicated inference + rollout/change mgmt)
Date: 2026-02-14
Start time: 4:00 PM PT
Duration: 47 min

Attendees
Redwood Inference: Dylan Brooks, Paula Mendes, Quentin Harris, Elliot Price
HelioHealth: Sarah Kim, Miguel Alvarez, Priya Desai, Jordan Blake

Auto-summary (generated)
- HelioHealth wants a Dedicated POC with predictable rollouts and explicit release notes whenever a model/version changes.
- Redwood described version pinning, canary rollouts, and the upcoming model changelog feature (schema-backed, auditable, with Console + docs outputs).
- Security topics: audit evidence, who can approve/publish notes, and retention expectations for regulated workflows.

Action items (verbatim)
- Paula to send a POC plan + proposed cadence (weekly review) (due 2/16)
- Elliot to send sample release-note template and what fields will be included (due 2/18)
- Miguel to send prompt set for eval + latency constraints (due 2/20)
- Priya to send HelioHealth CAB/change-management checklist (due 2/19)

----

[00:00] Dylan Brooks: Cool. Hey everyone. Thanks for making time on Friday. Um, goal today is to scope what a POC would look like, and make sure we understand the requirements, especially around rollouts and, like, change management.

[00:13] Sarah Kim: Sounds good.

[00:14] Paula Mendes: Yep.

[00:16] Dylan Brooks: Quick intros? I’m Dylan, engineering sponsor on the platform side. Paula runs the rollouts product area. Quentin is on our model catalog team. Elliot leads docs.

[00:27] Sarah Kim: I’m Sarah, data science director. Miguel is our ML engineer who’ll actually implement this. Priya is security and compliance. Jordan is our platform engineering manager.

[00:39] Miguel Alvarez: Hey.

[00:40] Priya Desai: Hi.

[00:41] Jordan Blake: Hey all.

[00:44] Dylan Brooks: Great. Maybe Sarah, can you give the two-minute context? What are you trying to achieve and what went wrong with prior attempts.

[00:53] Sarah Kim: Yeah. We’re rolling out a clinical note summarization feature. We’ve prototyped with a couple vendors. The recurring issue is… the model behavior changes and we find out after the fact, and then it triggers an internal incident because we have a regulated workflow. We have to document changes, do approvals. Even if it’s “minor,” we need a release note or something we can attach.

[01:19] Sarah Kim: So for POC, success is: predictable performance, yes, but also predictable rollouts. And, like, we need to receive release notes for any model or version changes. Ideally machine readable.

[01:33] Paula Mendes: Got it. When you say “receive,” do you mean email, webhook, RSS, API, Console…?

[01:40] Sarah Kim: Honestly any. But we’d prefer a feed we can integrate. At minimum a page we can link internally.

[01:47] Miguel Alvarez: Also version pinning. Like if we pin “model X version Y,” we want to be confident it’s actually that exact thing.

[01:56] Dylan Brooks: Yep. That’s a big theme in what we’re building right now.

[02:00] Priya Desai: And on the compliance side, we need evidence of who changed what and when. Not necessarily all internal details, but an audit trail.

[02:10] Quentin Harris: Makes sense.

[02:12] Dylan Brooks: Cool. Let’s break it into POC scope: deployment mode, models, and the rollout/release note workflow.

[02:19] Jordan Blake: Before that, can you confirm what deployment options we’d be testing? We’ve been burned by hosted APIs where data retention is unclear.

[02:28] Dylan Brooks: Sure. For HelioHealth, given the regulated context, we typically recommend Dedicated. That’s reserved GPU capacity, isolated at the tenant level. Still managed by us, but you get predictable throughput and isolation. We can also do Private (VPC) but that’s usually longer lead time.

[02:50] Priya Desai: Dedicated is still multi-tenant hardware though, right?

[02:54] Dylan Brooks: It’s dedicated pools per customer. Under the hood it’s our fleet, but logically and operationally isolated. We can go deeper on details in a security review; we have standard language around it.

[03:08] Priya Desai: Okay.

[03:10] Paula Mendes: And from a rollout perspective, Dedicated gives us more control for canaries, because capacity is predictable. Hosted can do canaries too, but you can get contention.

[03:21] Miguel Alvarez: So dedicated seems right.

[03:23] Dylan Brooks: Great. Now models: Miguel, what are you calling? Chat completions? Summarization? Any tool calling.

[03:31] Miguel Alvarez: It’s like, instruction following. Input is mixed: structured fields plus free text. Output is structured summary with sections. We’ve done JSON schema style outputs. Tool calling not necessary, but structured output is.

[03:50] Quentin Harris: Okay. Context window needs? Like how long are the notes.

[03:54] Miguel Alvarez: Sometimes 10k tokens-ish. We want headroom. Also some are short but we’d like stable latency.

[04:04] Quentin Harris: Got it. So likely a model that handles 16k+ comfortably. We can propose a few candidates.

[04:11] Sarah Kim: We’ve used Azure OpenAI for the prototype, but… we can’t get the change notifications we need.

[04:18] Dylan Brooks: Understood.

[04:20] Paula Mendes: On our side, what we’re rolling out is a model metadata standard plus a customer-visible changelog. It’s specifically meant to stop the “silent change” problem.

[04:32] Jordan Blake: Is that live today or coming soon.

[04:35] Paula Mendes: Parts are in beta internally. For POC we can do a couple things: (1) we can guarantee version pinning at the API level. (2) we can share draft release note format for anything we change during the POC. (3) if you’re okay being a beta design partner, we can enable you early when the Console tab is ready.

[04:58] Sarah Kim: That sounds like what we want.

[05:00] Elliot Price: And on the docs side, we’re standardizing the wording. So release notes will have consistent sections: what changed, impact, compatibility notes, deprecation timelines, and links to any metrics. No internal-only stuff.

[05:15] Priya Desai: We need to be careful. Some vendors put vague stuff like “minor improvements” and that’s not sufficient for our CAB.

[05:22] Elliot Price: Yep, heard. We can make it specific without leaking internals. For example, “Updated tokenizer version” or “Changed default sampling parameters” would be explicit. If it’s performance-only, we call that out as “no functional output change expected,” but we try not to over-claim.

[05:41] Miguel Alvarez: Wait, you can change sampling defaults without changing the version?

[05:46] Dylan Brooks: In our model registry approach, any customer-visible change to behavior should be represented as a versioned change event. The whole point is to make the thing you pin actually immutable.

[05:58] Quentin Harris: There are edge cases like infrastructure-level improvements that affect latency but not outputs—those can be recorded as perf notes rather than a new model version. But it still goes into the changelog.

[06:13] Sarah Kim: That’s fine. We still need to know if latency changes or if there’s a kernel update. Actually latency changes matter too because we have timeouts.

[06:23] Dylan Brooks: Totally.

[06:24] Paula Mendes: Let’s define what “predictable rollout” means for you. Is it: no unannounced changes, ability to pin, ability to do canaries, and a rollback plan.

[06:34] Sarah Kim: Yes. Also, deprecation notices. If you’re going to deprecate a model, we need like 90 days.

[06:41] Priya Desai: And evidence we got notified. Like a dated entry.

[06:46] Paula Mendes: We can include deprecation fields: sunset date, replacement model, and customer messaging.

[06:55] Jordan Blake: And can the entry be immutable? Like if someone edits it later, do we see history?

[07:02] Dylan Brooks: The plan is to treat published entries as immutable. Corrections are handled as “superseding entries” with history preserved.

[07:11] Priya Desai: Good. That’s exactly what auditors ask.

[07:15] Miguel Alvarez: How do we consume it? Like an endpoint.

[07:19] Quentin Harris: The roadmap includes a JSON feed endpoint and an RSS/Atom feed. And the API responses will also include the resolved model version and a link to the changelog entry.

[07:31] Miguel Alvarez: So in the completion response we can log “model_version=… changelog_url=…”?

[07:37] Quentin Harris: Exactly.

[07:39] Sarah Kim: That helps.

[07:41] Dylan Brooks: For the POC, we can do a lightweight version: we’ll pin a specific model version, and we’ll agree there will be no changes to that version during the POC unless you approve it, and if we do we’ll produce a release note.

[07:55] Paula Mendes: And we can set up a canary rollout if you want to test an update: e.g., 5% traffic to candidate version, compare metrics, then ramp.

[08:05] Jordan Blake: Does that happen via Console or API.

[08:09] Paula Mendes: Both, but in beta it’s mostly Console-driven with audit logging.

[08:14] Miguel Alvarez: We’d likely automate from our side eventually.

[08:17] Dylan Brooks: Understood.

[08:19] Sarah Kim: Can you talk about what constitutes a “model change event”? Like does changing quantization count.

[08:26] Quentin Harris: Yes. Quantization profile, tokenizer, weights, context length, tool compatibility—those are versioned metadata. If any of those change, we consider it a new version and it should produce a changelog entry.

[08:41] Miguel Alvarez: Nice.

[08:43] Priya Desai: Are there any fields you won’t expose.

[08:46] Elliot Price: Yes, internal-only fields are kept internal. But customer-facing includes identity, compatibility, deprecation, and high-level performance notes. We’ll share a template.

[09:00] Jordan Blake: Okay. Switching gears: performance targets for POC. We need p95 under, like, 2 seconds for typical notes? That may be impossible for 10k tokens.

[09:12] Miguel Alvarez: Yeah to be precise: We have two paths. One is short note classification, small output. The other is long summarization with output ~700 tokens. For long, p95 10–12 seconds could be okay, but it has to be stable. No random 60s.

[09:30] Dylan Brooks: That’s helpful. Dedicated will help stabilize the tail.

[09:34] Quentin Harris: Also we can tune batching and caching; but for POC we’ll keep it simple and predictable.

[09:41] Sarah Kim: Another requirement: We need to stage changes. We have dev/staging/prod. Ideally model version pin in each.

[09:49] Paula Mendes: We can set separate projects or environments, and you can pin different versions per environment.

[09:56] Miguel Alvarez: Great.

[09:58] Dylan Brooks: Priya, any security constraints we should know now so we don’t propose something you can’t run.

[10:05] Priya Desai: Yep. PHI. We require encryption in transit. We prefer customer-managed keys, but for POC maybe standard is fine if you have SOC2 and we can review. Also need audit logs. Not for every token, but for admin actions and changes.

[10:24] Dylan Brooks: Got it. We’ll send the standard security pack. For audit logs: the changelog publishing and model metadata changes will have audit events, and the rollout actions too.

[10:36] Priya Desai: And retention. Like how long do you keep those logs.

[10:41] Dylan Brooks: In general we can retain for enterprise tiers; for POC we can outline the baseline. Let’s capture your requirement.

[10:48] Priya Desai: One year minimum.

[10:51] Dylan Brooks: Okay.

[10:53] Paula Mendes: Also, for the release notes themselves, we can keep them indefinitely and treat them as immutable records.

[11:01] Sarah Kim: Great.

[11:03] Miguel Alvarez: On the structured output: do you support JSON schema or function calling.

[11:08] Quentin Harris: We support structured outputs, and for some models we support tool/function calling compatibility. For your use case, we can enforce JSON outputs with constraints. We’ll pick a model that’s good at that.

[11:21] Miguel Alvarez: Good.

[11:23] Jordan Blake: How do rollbacks work if you publish a new version and it’s worse.

[11:30] Paula Mendes: Rollouts are policy-driven. You can set a fallback model version. If error rates or latency exceed thresholds, it can auto-fallback. Or manual rollback.

[11:42] Jordan Blake: That’s important.

[11:44] Sarah Kim: In our org, we have to be able to show that we rolled back. So it should be logged.

[11:50] Paula Mendes: Yes. Rollout actions are audit logged.

[11:54] Priya Desai: Who can approve a release note from your side.

[11:59] Elliot Price: Internally we’ll have a workflow: draft, in review, published. Usually product plus release engineering sign off. For customer-visible wording, docs will review too.

[12:12] Priya Desai: Okay. That’s good governance.

[12:15] Dylan Brooks: Let’s anchor on the POC plan. My suggestion: 2 to 3 weeks, Dedicated capacity. Week 1 is integration and baseline. Week 2 is eval and tuning. Optional week 3 is testing a canary update to validate the release note + approval flow.

[12:35] Sarah Kim: I like the idea of testing the workflow. Because that’s the differentiator for us.

[12:40] Miguel Alvarez: Agreed.

[12:42] Jordan Blake: What do you need from us.

[12:45] Quentin Harris: Prompt set. Ideally 30–50 representative prompts for both short and long. Also “bad cases.” If you have a rubric that’s even better.

[12:56] Miguel Alvarez: We can do that.

[12:58] Elliot Price: And on the release notes, we’ll share a template and an example entry so you can see the level of specificity.

[13:07] Priya Desai: Please include: date/time, model ID, version ID, what changed, impact, rollback instructions, deprecation if relevant, and contact.

[13:19] Elliot Price: Yep, that’s aligned.

[13:22] Paula Mendes: Also compatibility: context window, tool calling support, structured output notes.

[13:28] Sarah Kim: Great.

[13:30] Dylan Brooks: Any other vendor comparisons we should know. You mentioned Azure.

[13:35] Sarah Kim: Azure OpenAI is the incumbent. We tested Anthropic direct as well. And we looked at Together, but we weren’t sure about auditability.

[13:47] Miguel Alvarez: And we tried self-hosted vLLM but ops overhead is high.

[13:52] Dylan Brooks: Makes sense. Our pitch is exactly: predictable serving with operational tooling.

[13:58] Jordan Blake: Are you going to require us to upgrade SDKs often.

[14:02] Quentin Harris: No. We try to keep API stable. But we will expose additional fields like “resolved model version” and “changelog URL.” That should be backwards compatible.

[14:14] Miguel Alvarez: Nice.

[14:16] Paula Mendes: Another question: how do you want to be notified? For POC we can do email and a link. Longer term, feed.

[14:24] Sarah Kim: Email to a distro is fine, plus a link. Long term, JSON feed.

[14:30] Priya Desai: And we’ll need to archive it.

[14:33] Elliot Price: The docs page will be stable, and the entry can be exported as JSON. We can make sure it’s easy to capture.

[14:43] Dylan Brooks: Let’s also talk about “no silent changes.” The contract we can make in Dedicated is: the model version you pin is immutable. If we have to hotfix something, it becomes a new version with a changelog entry. Your pinned version stays pinned.

[14:59] Miguel Alvarez: That’s the key point.

[15:01] Sarah Kim: And do you ever re-label versions.

[15:05] Quentin Harris: No. Versions are stable IDs.

[15:09] Priya Desai: Good.

[15:11] Jordan Blake: Okay. What about regionality? Are we pinned to a region.

[15:16] Dylan Brooks: For Dedicated, yes, region selection is part of the deployment. If you want DR in another region, that’s a separate discussion.

[15:27] Jordan Blake: For POC, one region is fine.

[15:30] Dylan Brooks: Great.

[15:32] (crosstalk)

[15:33] Paula Mendes: Sorry, quick one: do you need approvals on your side before any rollout.

[15:39] Sarah Kim: Yes. We have an internal CAB meeting weekly. So if you plan changes, we need them before Wednesday.

[15:48] Paula Mendes: Okay. For the optional canary test, we’ll schedule it around that.

[15:55] Dylan Brooks: Perfect.

[16:00] Miguel Alvarez: One more: is there a way for us to programmatically fetch the release notes. Like if we run a nightly job.

[16:08] Quentin Harris: Yes, that’s the JSON feed idea. For the POC, we can give you a staging endpoint or even just a signed URL to a JSON artifact.

[16:18] Miguel Alvarez: Great.

[16:20] Priya Desai: Signed URL is okay but we’d prefer auth.

[16:23] Dylan Brooks: Understood. We can use API keys for POC.

[16:28] Elliot Price: And we’ll keep language customer-safe. No internal codenames.

[16:33] Sarah Kim: Thank you.

[16:35] Dylan Brooks: Let’s define success metrics. Sarah said predictable rollouts + release notes. On model quality: what’s the bar.

[16:44] Sarah Kim: We have a clinical QA rubric. We’ll do manual review for POC. We mainly need consistency and no hallucinated meds. We’ll flag critical errors.

[16:57] Miguel Alvarez: Technically we also need the output schema to be valid JSON, like 99.5%+

[17:03] Quentin Harris: Okay.

[17:05] Dylan Brooks: Latency: you mentioned 10–12 seconds for long. For short, what’s the expectation.

[17:12] Miguel Alvarez: Under 2 seconds p95 would be ideal for short.

[17:18] Dylan Brooks: Great.

[17:20] Jordan Blake: Throughput wise, we can start small. Maybe 5 RPS.

[17:24] Dylan Brooks: That’s fine for POC.

[17:27] Paula Mendes: For Dedicated sizing, we’ll propose something that meets that with headroom.

[17:33] Dylan Brooks: Okay. Timeline: when do you want to start.

[17:37] Sarah Kim: We’d like to start within two weeks. We have an internal demo early March.

[17:44] Dylan Brooks: Okay that’s doable.

[17:46] Priya Desai: We’ll need security review concurrently.

[17:50] Dylan Brooks: We can do that.

[17:52] Elliot Price: I’ll send the release note example early next week so you can incorporate into your internal process.

[17:59] Sarah Kim: Great.

[18:01] Paula Mendes: Also, we can share screenshots of the upcoming Console changelog tab, even if it’s not enabled yet.

[18:08] Jordan Blake: That would help.

[18:10] Miguel Alvarez: Yeah.

[18:12] Dylan Brooks: Any other concerns.

[18:14] Sarah Kim: Just one: If something changes in the runtime, like kernel updates, do we get notified.

[18:22] Quentin Harris: Yes, there’s alignment between runtime notes and model notes. If runtime changes materially impact a model’s performance, we link it. For output behavior, we treat it carefully.

[18:35] Sarah Kim: Okay.

[18:37] Priya Desai: For audits we’ll want the “what changed” to be not purely marketing.

[18:43] Elliot Price: 100%.

[18:45] Dylan Brooks: Cool. Let’s do a recap and next steps.

[18:49] Dylan Brooks: Redwood will send: a POC plan with timeline, dedicated sizing, and success metrics. Elliot will send sample release notes template and one example entry. Quentin will propose model candidates and pinning approach.

[19:07] Dylan Brooks: HelioHealth will send: prompt set for eval, and Priya will send your CAB requirements including notice window and required fields.

[19:19] Sarah Kim: Yes.

[19:20] Miguel Alvarez: Yep.

[19:21] Priya Desai: Yes.

[19:22] Jordan Blake: Works.

[19:24] Dylan Brooks: Great. We’ll schedule a deeper technical session next week to cover dedicated rollouts and audit logging in detail.

[19:33] Paula Mendes: I’ll coordinate times.

[19:35] Dylan Brooks: Thanks everyone.

[19:37] Sarah Kim: Thanks.

[19:38] (Meeting ends)

Note: Fireflies transcript may be truncated; timestamps after ~19:40 reflect the recorded portion exported to this artifact.
